fallback.text: A 68-year-old woman with fever, rigors and confusion has a 40 % chance of bacterial sepsis and a 60 % chance of a viral illness. A raised lactate is four in five times present in sepsis and one in ten times in a viral illness, so it lifts the probability of sepsis from 40 % to 84 %. Drawn early with blood cultures, it leads to antibiotics within the hour and two litres of fluid: the mean arterial pressure stays above 75 mmHg, the lactate falls to 1.3 mmol/L and the patient stabilises. Without antibiotics the infection grows: after about four hours the mean pressure falls below 65 mmHg, the lactate climbs past 3 mmol/L and she is in septic shock. A CT scan instead of the lactate costs fifteen times more and still leaves the sepsis untreated, the trap of premature closure. The picture shows both courses side by side.
